documents.content:
# OpenTitan Earl Grey Chip Specification

This document describes the OpenTitan Earl Grey chip functionality in detail.
For an overview, refer to the [OpenTitan Earl Grey Chip Datasheet](../datasheet.md).

# Theory of Operations

The netlist `chip_earlgrey_asic` contains the features listed above and is intended for ASIC synthesis, whereas the netlist `chip_earlgrey_cw310` provides an emulation environment for the `cw310` FPGA board.
The code for Ibex is developed in its own [lowRISC repo](https://github.com/lowrisc/ibex), and is [*vendored in*](../../../../doc/contributing/hw/vendor.md) to this repository.
Surrounding Ibex is a suite of *Comportable* peripherals that follow the [Comportability Guidelines](../../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md) for lowRISC peripheral IP.
Each of these IP has its own specification.
See the table produced in the [hardware documentation page](../../../README.md) for links to those specifications.

## Design Details

This section provides some details for the processor and the peripherals.
See their representative specifications for more information.
This section also contains a brief overview of some of the features of the final product.

### Clocking and Reset

Clocks and resets are supplied from the Analog Sensor Top, referred to as [ast](../../ip/ast/README.md)) from this point onwards in the document.

`ast` supplies a number of clocks into `top_earlgrey`.
- sys: main jittery system clock used for higher performance blocks and security (processor, memory and crypto blocks).
- io: a fixed clock used for peripheral blocks such as timers and I/O functionality, such as SPI or I2C.
- usb: a fixed clock used specifically for usb operations.
- aon: an always on, low frequency clock used for power management and low speed timers.

These clocks are then divided down and distributed to the rest of the system.
See [clock manager](../../ip_autogen/clkmgr/README.md)) for more details.

`ast` also supplies a number of power-okay signals to `top_earlgrey`, and these are used as asynchronous root resets.
- vcaon_pok: The always on domain of the system is ready.
- vcmain_pok: The main operating domain of the system is ready.

When one of these power-okay signals drop, the corresponding domain in `top_earlgrey` is reset.
Please refer to [reset manager](../../ip_autogen/rstmgr/README.md)) for more details.
Resets throughout the design are asynchronous active low as per the Comportability specification.

Once reset, the reset vector begins in ROM, whose job is to validate code in the embedded flash before jumping to it.
Valid code is assumed to have been instantiated into the flash, if not, the ROM shuts down the device unless prompted to bootstrap.

There are multiple avenues to load valid code into the flash:
1. JTAG initiated flash programming.
2. ROM bootstrap

#### AST Clocking and Reset Relationship

While the ast supplies clocks and resets to the `top_earlgrey`, it also contains additional functions that interact with the design.
These include the `RNG`, `ADC`, jittery clock controls and an assortment of other sensors.
The operating clocks and resets for these interfaces are supplied by the device in order to ensure correct synchronous operations.
The clock mapping is shown below:

| AST Port         | `top_earlgrey` Clock     |
|------------------|--------------------------|
| clk_ast_adc_i    | aon                      |
| clk_ast_alert_i  | io_div4                  |
| clk_ast_es_i     | sys                      |
| clk_ast_rng_i    | sys                      |
| clk_ast_tlul_i   | io_div4                  |
| clk_ast_usb_i    | usb                      |

The reset clock domain is identical to the table above, and the power domain mapping is shown below


| AST Port         | `top_earlgrey` Power Domain |
|------------------|-----------------------------|
| rst_ast_adc_i    | always-on                   |
| rst_ast_alert_i  | main                        |
| rst_ast_es_i     | main                        |
| rst_ast_rng_i    | main                        |
| rst_ast_tlul_i   | main                        |
| rst_ast_usb_i    | main                        |

### System Reset Handling and Flash

Since `top_earlgrey` contains flash, it is important to examine the memory's relationship with resets.

For flash, resets that occur during a stateful operation (program or erase) must be carefully handled to ensure the flash memory is not damaged.
There are three reset scenarios:

* Reset due to external supply lowering.
* Reset due to internal peripheral request.
* Reset due to lower power entry and exit.

#### Reset due to External Supply

Device resets due to supply dropping below a specific threshold are commonly known as "brown-out".
When this occurs, the flash memory must go through specialized sequencing to ensure the cells are not damaged.
This process is handled exclusively between ast and the flash.
Please see the [relevant section](../../ip/ast/README.md#main-vcc-power-detection-and-flash-protection) for more details.

#### Reset due to Internal Request

When the device receives an internal request to reset (for example [aon_timer](../../../ip/aon_timer/README.md#aon-watchdog-timer)), device power is kept on and the flash is directly reset.
It is assumed that the flash device, when powered, will be able to correctly handle such a sequence and properly protect itself.

#### Reset due to Low Power Entry

When the device receives a low power entry request while flash activity is ongoing, the [pwrmgr](../../ip_autogen/pwrmgr/README.md#abort-handling)) is responsible for ensuring the entry request is aborted.


### Main processor (`core_ibex`)

The main processor (`core_ibex`) is a small and efficient, 32-bit, in-order RISC-V core with a 2-stage pipeline that implements the RV32IMC instruction set architecture.
It was initially developed as part of the [PULP platform](https://www.pulp-platform.org) under the name "Zero-riscy" [\[1\]](https://doi.org/10.1109/PATMOS.2017.8106976), and has been contributed to [lowRISC](https://www.lowrisc.org) who maintains it and develops it further.
See the [core_ibex specification](https://ibex-core.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) for more details of the core.
In addition to the standard RISC-V functionality, Ibex implements M (machine) and U (user) mode per the RISC-V standard.
Attached to the Ibex core are a debug module (DM) and interrupt module (PLIC).

#### JTAG / Debug module

One feature available for Earl Grey processor core is debug access.
By interfacing with JTAG pins, logic in the debug module allows the core to enter debug mode (per RISC-V 0.13 debug spec), and gives the design the ability to inject code either into the device - by emulating an instruction - or into memory.
Full details can be found in the [rv_dm specification](../../../ip/rv_dm/README.md).

#### Interrupt Controller

Adjacent to the Ibex core is an interrupt controller that implements the RISC-V PLIC standard.
This accepts a vector of interrupt sources within the device, and assigns leveling and priority to them before sending to the core for handling.
See the details in the [rv_plic specification](../../ip_autogen/rv_plic/README.md).

#### Performance

Ibex currently achieves a [CoreMark](https://www.eembc.org/coremark/) per MHz of 1.93 on Earl Grey.
For a detailed analysis of where this number comes from, please refer to this [GitHub issue](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/17370#issuecomment-1453324348).
In short, by [moving read-only data from Flash into SRAM](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/17370#issuecomment-1446719338) and by playing with optimization flags, A CoreMark/MHz of 2.15 is achievable.
This number is close to the maximum achievable number for Ibex with an ideal single-cycle access memory system when using the LLVM compiler.

When switching to GCC and combining the Ibex configuration used in OpenTitan Earl Grey with an idealistic single-cycle access Flash memory, a CoreMark/MHz number of 3.07 is achievable.
To achieve this performance, CoreMark can be compiled with GCC 9.2.0 and with the following flags: `-march=rv32imc -mabi=ilp32 -mcmodel=medany -mtune=sifive-3-series -O3 -falign-functions=16 -funroll-all-loops -finline-functions -falign-jumps=4 -mstrict-align` .

The Ibex documentation has more details on the current pipeline operation, including stall behaviour for each instruction in the [Pipeline Details](https://ibex-core.readthedocs.io/en/latest/03_reference/pipeline_details.html) section.

### Memory

The device contains three memory address spaces for instruction and data.

Instruction ROM (32kB) is the target for the Ibex processor after release of external reset.
The ROM contains hard-coded instructions whose purpose is to do a minimal subset of platform checking before checking the next stage of code.
The next stage - a boot loader stored in embedded flash memory - is the first piece of code that is not hard-coded into the silicon of the device, and thus must be signature checked.
The ROM executes this signature check by implementing a RSA-check algorithm on the full contents of the boot loader.
The details of this check will come at a later date.
For verification execute-time reasons, this RSA check will be overridable in the FPGA and verification platforms (details TBD).
This is part of the *Secure Boot Process* that will be detailed in a security section in the future.

Earl Grey contains 1024kB of embedded-flash (e-flash) memory for code storage.
This is intended to house the boot loader mentioned above, as well as the operating system and application that layers on top.
At this time there is no operating system provided; applications are simple proof of concept code to show that the chip can do with a bare-metal framework.

Embedded-flash is the intended technology for a silicon design implementing the full OpenTitan device.
It has interesting and challenging parameters that are unique to the technology that the silicon is implemented in.
Earl Grey, as an FPGA proof of concept, will model these parameters in its emulation of the memory in order to prepare for the replacement with the silicon flash macros that will come.
This includes the read-speeds, the page-sized erase and program interfaces, the two-bank update scheme, and the non-volatile nature of the memory.
Since by definition these details can't be finalized until a silicon technology node is chosen, these can only be emulated in the FPGA environment.
We will choose parameters that are considered roughly equivalent of the state of the art embedded-flash macros on the market today.

Details on how e-flash memory is used by software will be detailed in future Secure Boot Process and Software sections over time.

The intent is for the contents of the embedded flash code to survive FPGA reset as it would as a NVM in silicon.
Loading of the FPGA with initial content, or updating with new content, is described in other software specifications.
The SPI device peripheral is provided as a method to bulk-load e-flash memory.
The processor debug port (via JTAG) is also available for code loading.
See those specifications for more details.

Also included is a 128kB of SRAM available for data storage (stack, heap, etc.) by the Ibex processor.
It is also available for code storage, though that is not its intended purpose.

The base address of the ROM, Flash, and SRAM are given in the address map section later in this document.

### Secure boot

Earlgrey follows the [Secure Boot](../../../../doc/security/specs/secure_boot/README.md) specification. The `ROM` has 3 key slots
which are allocated as follows:

| Slot | Role | Name |
|------|------|------|
| 0 | test | `test 0` |
| 1 | test | `test 1` |
| 2 | dev | `dev 0` |
| 3 | dev | `dev 1` |
| 4 | prod | `prod 0` |
| 5 | prod | `prod 1` |
| 6 | prod | `prod 2` |

### Peripherals

Earl Grey contains a suite of "peripherals", or subservient execution units connected to the Ibex processor by means of a bus interconnect.
Each of these peripherals follows an interface scheme dictated in the [Comportability Specification.](../../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md).
That specification details how the processor communicates with the peripheral (via TLUL interconnect); how the peripheral communicates with the chip IO (via fixed or multiplexable IO); how the peripheral communicates with the processor (interrupts); and how the peripheral communicates security events (via alerts).
See that specification for generic details on this scheme.

#### Chip IO Peripherals

##### Pin Multiplexor Module (`pinmux`)

The pin multiplexor's purpose is to route between peripherals and the available multiplexable IO of the chip.
At this time, the pin multiplexor is provided, but it is not used to its full potential.
In addition, the multiplexor device manages control or pad attributes like drive strength, technology (OD, OS, etc), pull up, pull down, etc., of the chip's external IO.
It is notable that there are many differences between an FPGA implementation of Earl Grey and an ASIC version when it comes to pins and pads.
Some pad attributes with analog characteristics like drive strength, slew rate and Open Drain technology are not supported on all platforms.

The pin multiplexor is a peripheral on the TLUL bus, with collections of registers that provide software configurability.
See the [pinmux specification](../../../ip/pinmux/README.md) for how to connect peripheral IO to chip IO and for information on pad control features.

##### UART

The chip contains one UART peripheral that implement single-lane duplex UART functionality.
The outputs and inputs can be configured to any chip IO via the [pinmux](../../../ip/pinmux/README.md).

See the [UART specification](../../../ip/uart/README.md) for more details on this peripheral.

##### GPIO

The chip contains one GPIO peripheral that creates 32 bits of bidirectional communication with the outside world via the pinmux.
Via pinmux any of the 32 pins of GPIO can be connected to any of the 32 MIO chip pins, in any direction.
See the [GPIO specification](../../../ip/gpio/README.md) for more details on this peripheral.
See the [pinmux specification](../../../ip/pinmux/README.md) for how to connect peripheral IO to chip IO.

##### SPI device


The SPI device implements multiple modes:
- Firmware mode
- TPM mode
- Flash mode
- Passthrough mode

Firmware Mode is a generic data transfer mode.
It can be used by software to construct a simple firmware upgrade mechanism for in-field devices.

TPM mode supports SPI transfers in compliance with the TPM PC Client Platform.
The interface is single data lane and supports built-in data back pressuring.

Flash mode supports serial flash emulation.
Typical commands such as read status, address mode, read data and program data are either natively supported or can be emulated.

Passthrough mode supports serial flash passthrough from an upstream SPI host to a downstream serial flash device.

See the [SPI device specification](../../../ip/spi_device/README.md) for more details.

##### USB device

The chip contains a single module that supports USB device mode at full speed.
In addition to normal functionality, USB suspend / resume is supported alongside the chip's low power modes.

See the [USB device specification](../../../ip/usbdev/README.md) for more details.

##### I2C host

In order to be able to command I2C devices on systems where Earl Grey will be included, I2C host functionality will be required.
This will include standard, full, and fast mode, up to 1Mbaud.
More details of the I2C host module will come in a later specification update.
The pins of the I2C host will be available to connect to any of the multiplexable IO (MIO) of the Earl Grey device.
More than one I2C host module might be instantiated in the top level.

#### Security Peripherals

##### AES

[AES](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/fips/nist.fips.197.pdf) is the primary [symmetric encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric-key_algorithm) and decryption mechanism used in OpenTitan protocols.
AES runs with key sizes of 128b, 192b, or 256b.
The module can select encryption or decryption of data that arrives in 16 byte quantities to be encrypted or decrypted using different block cipher modes of operation.
It supports [ECB mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_cipher_mode_of_operation#ECB), [CBC mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_cipher_mode_of_operation#CBC), [CFB mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_cipher_mode_of_operation#CFB), [OFB mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_cipher_mode_of_operation#OFB) and [CTR mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_cipher_mode_of_operation#CTR).

The [GCM mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_cipher_mode_of_operation#GCM) is not implemented in hardware, but can be constructed using AES in counter mode.
The integrity tag calculation can be implemented in Ibex and accelerated via bitmanip instructions.

Details on how to write key and data material into the peripheral, how to initiate encryption and decryption, and how to read out results, are available in the [AES specification](../../../ip/aes/README.md).

##### SHA-256/HMAC

SHA-256 is the primary
[hashing algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptographic_hash_function) used in OpenTitan protocols.
SHA-256 is a member of the [SHA-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2) family of hashing algorithms, where the digest (or hash output) is of 256b length, regardless of the data size of the input to be hashed.
The data is sent into the SHA peripheral after declaring the beginning of a hash request (effectively zeroing out the internal state to initial conditions), 32b at a time.
Once all data has been sent, the user can indicate the completion of the hash request (with optional partial-word final write).
The peripheral produces the hash result available for register read by the user.
All data transfer is processor-available, i.e. data is passed into the module via register writes.

[HMAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMAC) is a message authentication protocol layered on top of a hashing function (in this case SHA-256), mixing in a secret key for cryptographic purposes.
HMAC is a particular application of appending the secret key in a prescribed manner, twice, around the hashing (via SHA-256) of the message.

Details on how to write key and data material into the peripheral, how to initiate hashing / authentication, and how to read out results, are available in the [SHA/HMAC specification](../../../ip/hmac/README.md).

##### Alert Handler

Alerts, as defined in the [Comportability Specification](../../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md), are defined as security-sensitive interrupts that need to be handled in a timely manner to respond to a security threat.
Unlike standard interrupts, they are not solely handled by software.
Alerts trigger a first-stage request to be handled by software in the standard mode as interrupts, but trigger a second-stage response by the alert handler if software is not able to respond.
This ensures that the underlying concern is guaranteed to be addressed if the processor is busy, wedged, or itself under attack.

Each peripheral has an option to present a list of individual alerts, representing individual threats that require handling.
These alerts are sent in a particular encoding method to the alert handler module, itself a peripheral on the system bus.
See the details of the alert handler specification for more information.

##### TRNG entropy source

Randomness is a critical part of any security chip.
It provides variations in execution that can keep attackers from predicting when the best time is to attack.
It provides secret material used for identity and cryptographic purposes.
It can be seeded into algorithmic computation to obscure sensitive data values.
In short, it is a source of critical functionality that must be designed to be truly random, but also free from attack itself.

Most [TRNG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardware_random_number_generator)s (True Random Number Generators) are analog designs, taking advantage of some physical event or process that is non-deterministic.
Example designs rely on metastability, electronic noise, timing variations, thermal noise, quantum variation, etc.
These are then filtered and sent into a pool of entropy that the device can sample at any time, for whatever purposes are needed.
The creation, filtering, storage, protection, and dissemination of the randomness are all deep topics of intense research in their own right.

The primary interface to the entropy pool is a read request of available random bits.
The TRNG interface can indicate how many bits are available, and then software can read from this pool, if available.
Reading of entropy that is not available should immediately trigger an interrupt or an alert.

Since silicon is required to contain an analog design tied to the final chosen silicon technology process, our FPGA implementation can only approximate the results.
We however fully specify the software interface to the TRNG in a digital wrapper.
In FPGA we emulate the randomness with something akin to a [PRBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence).

#### Other peripherals

##### Timer(s)

Timers are critical for operating systems to ensure guaranteed performance for users.
To some level they are even required by the RISC-V specification.
At this time, one timer is provided, a 64b free running timer with a guaranteed (within a certain percentage) frequency.
A second one acting as a watchdog timer that can be used to backstop the processor in the case of it being unresponsive (usually due to development code that is wedged, rather than for instance due to security attack) will be provided in the future.
The goal is for both of these to be satisfied with the same timer module.

The specification for the timer can be found [here](../../../ip/rv_timer/README.md).

##### Flash Controller

The final peripheral discussed in this release of the netlist is an emulated flash controller.
As mentioned in the memory section, up to 1024kB of emulated embedded flash is available for code and data storage.
The primary read path for this data is in the standard memory address space.
Writes to that address space are ignored, however, since one can not write to flash in a standard way.
Instead, to write to flash, software must interact with the flash controller.

Flash functionality include three primary commands: read, erase, and program.
Read, as mentioned above, is standard, and uses the chip memory address space.
Erase is done at a page level, where the page size is parameterizable in the flash controller.
Upon receiving an erase request, the flash controller wipes all contents of that page, rendering the data in all `1`s state (`0xFFFFFFFF` per word).
Afterwards, software can program individual words to any value.
It is notable that software can continue to attempt to program words even before another erase, but it is not physically possible to return a flash bit back to a `'1'` state without another erase.
So future content is in effect an AND of the current content and the written value.

```
next_value = AND(current_value, write_word)
```

Erase and program are slow.
A typical erase time is measured in milliseconds, program times in microseconds.
The flash controller peripheral in this release approximates those expected times.

Security is also a concern, since secret data can be stored in the flash.
Some memory protection is provided by the flash controller.
For more details see the [flash controller module specification](../../ip_autogen/flash_ctrl/README.md).

### Interconnection

Interconnecting the processor and peripheral and memory units is a bus network built upon the TileLink-Uncached-Light protocol.
See the [OpenTitan bus specification](../../../ip/tlul/README.md) for more details.

#### Topology
`top_earlgrey` has a two-level hierarchy for its bus network.
Close to the CPU is the high-speed cluster, with low access latency.
Farther from the CPU, through a low-speed bridge, is the low-speed cluster, with higher access latency.

#### Performance

The following table describes the typical number of CPU cycles from a transaction's launch to its completion for a device in the specified cluster.
Note that these values assume there is no bus contention.

| Cluster    | CPU Access Latency |
| ---------- | ------------------ |
| High speed | 2 CPU cycles       |
| Low speed  | 18-20 CPU cycles   |

- If SRAM is placed at 0, accesses to data located within 2KB of 0x0 can be accomplished with a single instruction and thus reduce code size.

For the purpose of `top_earlgrey`, the first option has been chosen to benefit software development and testing

## Entropy Distribution Network

`top_earlgrey` has two [EDN](../../../ip/edn/README.md) instances, which are connected to one [CSRNG](../../../ip/csrng/README.md) instance (which in turn is connected to one [Entropy Source](../../../ip/entropy_src/README.md) instance).
The first EDN instance, `u_edn0`, has eight endpoints, which are connected to: Key Manager, OTP Controller, Analog Sensor Top, KMAC Accelerator, Alert Handler, AES Accelerator, the `URND` port of OTBN, and the Ibex RISC-V Core.
The second EDN instance, `u_edn1`, has one endpoint that is connected to the `RND` port of OTBN and seven endpoints that are tied off.
The second EDN instance, `u_edn1` is intended to be configured to deliver highest-quality entropy, e.g., for the generation of cryptographic secrets.
The first EDN instance, `u_edn0` is intended to be configured to deliver entropy at a higher rate and thus slightly lower quality.

#### Open drain / virtual open drain

Pads of type **BidirOd** and **BidirStd** support **open drain** and **virtual open drain**, respectively.
When open drain or virtual open drain is enabled in pinmux's attributes for such a pad, the PMOS transistor that would otherwise drive the output high for a logic 1 is disabled.
Thus for a logic 1, the impedance of the pad is essentially the output impedance of the CMOS transistor pair (which is specified in the data sheet of the chip).

However, there still exists a parallel connection to the supply rail through a protection circuit.
Therefore:
- For **BidirOd** pads in open drain mode, the output protection circuit allows voltages that exceed the supply voltage.
  The maximum voltage that may be applied in this case is derived from the maximum voltage of the specific pad type (which is specified in the data sheet of the chip).
- For **BidirStd** pads, the maximum voltage that may be applied is the supply voltage (within tolerance, as specified in the data sheet of the chip).

All other pad types support neither open drain nor virtual open drain.


# RTL Implementation Notes

At this time, the top-level netlist for earlgrey is a combination of hand-written SystemVerilog RTL with auto-generated sections for wiring of comportability interfaces.
There is a script for this auto-generation, centered around the top-level descriptor file `top_earlgrey.hjson` found in the repository.
A full definition of this descriptor file, its features, and related scripting is forthcoming.
This tooling generates the interconnecting crossbar (via `TLUL`) as well as the instantiations at the top level.
It also feeds into this document generation to ensure that the chosen address locations are documented automatically using the data in the source files.

## Top Level vs Chip Targets

It should first be **NOTED** that there is some subtlety on the notion of hierarchy within the top level.
There is netlist automation to create the module `top_earlgrey` as indicated in sections of this specification that follow.
**On top** of that module, hierarchically in the repo, are chip level instantiation targets directed towards a particular use case.
This includes `chip_earlgrey_cw310` for use in FPGA, and `chip_earlgrey_asic` for use (eventually) in a silicon implementation.
These chip level targets will include the actual pads as needed by the target platform.
At the time of this writing the two are not in perfect synchronization, but the intention will be for them to be as identical as possible.
Where appropriate, including the block diagram below, notes will be provided where the hierarchy subtleties are explained.

## FPGA Platform

**TODO: This section needs to be updated once pin updates are complete.**

In the FPGA platform, the logic for the JTAG and the SPI device are multiplexed within `chip_earlgrey_cw310`.
This is done for ease of programming by the external host.

## References

 ultra-low-power RISC-V cores for Internet-of-Things applications."

 (PATMOS 2017)_](https://doi.org/10.1109/PATMOS.2017.8106976)

# OpenTitan serial I/O subsystem design and UVM verification problem

Build a specification-driven design and DV result for the selected serial I/O subsystem. The in-scope IP identities are `spi_host`, `spi_device`, `usbdev`. This is a bounded subsystem exercise using one pinned OpenTitan revision, not a request to implement all of Earlgrey or a claim that this subset is a standalone upstream top-level.

## Input authority and hierarchy

`spec.json` contains unchanged public system/architecture/module/behavior/register documents, normative register configuration, and an explicitly authored integration profile and module graph. The source manifest records which original prose bodies qualify the >512 KiB size floor. System background and whole-top context do not expand the implementation scope. Register HJSON and selected integration context do not count toward that floor. Upstream RTL, existing testplans, UVM code and answer obligations are not part of the exported input.

Use `integration_profile.json` to distinguish normative requirements, selected configuration, external environment assumptions, and proposed design choices. Use `module_graph.json` as an initial shared relationship map; source-check and refine it without silently converting a proposal to a proven contract. TL-UL/comportability documents constrain applicable interfaces; they do not by themselves require redesigning an entire SoC fabric. Retain concrete contradictions, missing dependencies and ambiguity with source anchors. Use the revised benchmark-author contract below for named issues. New gaps require precise local obligations, not blanket source-conflict blockers.

## Required design and verification outputs

1. Import the specification by path through LoopX. Persist every requirement and its provenance; work in bounded contexts and recover from durable state in fresh host sessions.
2. Create one shared module/interface/configuration graph for both tracks. Preserve boundary assumptions, clock/reset domains, address/register contracts, cross-module handshake and error behavior, and any unresolved ownership or composition obligations.
3. Design track: adopt or refine the available microarchitecture, propose explicit choices where the source permits them, and produce reviewable synthesizable RTL or a declared fixed-version IP binding. Produce real elaboration/lint/CDC evidence where tools and complete constraints permit it.
4. DV track: derive TP directly from the same specification and shared contract. Generate UVM transactions, sequencers/sequences, drivers, passive monitors, independent scoreboards, functional coverage, environment, test classes and top-level binding. Cover normal operations, boundaries, backpressure, reset/error paths, and the cross-module scenarios justified by the sources.
5. Join the two tracks only at the same accepted contract/configuration revision. Preserve all required composition work; a fragment is not a completed module. Run simulation only when a complete build and checker contract exists.
6. Report passed, failed, blocked and untested stages separately. Requirement extraction, test counts, generated files and smoke success are not coverage. Declare any percentage only from real simulator evidence using a frozen bin denominator; functional coverage and RTL code coverage are separate metrics.

## Execution and evaluation boundary

Start an installed LoopX capability in this input-only workspace with the selected Codex or TRAE host. Use public `dv_import`, `dv_next`, `dv_claim`, `dv_context`, `dv_submit` and relevant design/DV tools; do not manufacture state acceptance or direct database edits. The fixture is inert and does not automatically invoke models or EDA tools. Raw sessions, candidates, private state and logs belong in the execution workspace, never back in this public corpus.

An evaluator may compare outputs against a separately held pinned upstream reference implementation and verification material. Multiple correct RTL architectures and UVM organizations are acceptable; textual similarity is not the correctness criterion. File-only staging is not a claim of network/filesystem isolation from public upstream answers. Simulator/dependency qualification and any 90% target remain separate execution gates.

<!-- BEGIN SOURCE-ADJUDICATIONS -->
## Revised normative exercise contract

Benchmark-author policy: explicit declared field names, bit ranges, access types and selected integration configuration govern over obsolete narrative references. This is an authored exercise policy, not an attributed user instruction or a universal upstream priority rule. Conflicts inside HJSON and behavioral ambiguities use the individually named adjudications; no blanket HJSON-wins rule resolves them. Authored decisions supersede only their stated scope. Preserve original source bytes and provenance. Local open obligations gate only affected acceptance claims. Candidate/golden RTL and UVM are not specification authority. No correction is simulation or coverage evidence.

**[CADENCE execution contract](cadence_contract.md):** Implement the selected subsystem as self-contained synthesizable SystemVerilog with an independent SystemVerilog UVM/SVA environment. Cadence Xcelium/IMC and Jasper/Genus are the execution targets. Upstream RTL, build descriptions and tests are historical comparison material, not required build inputs or an independent golden for this authored contract.

The fixed top, logical bus, digital interfaces, clock/reset domains and physical abstraction in that contract are mandatory input. Use dv_generate_uvm(profile_path='eda/verification_profile.json'); complete and review eda/project.json for the staged Cadence runner. No upstream native build is required. No EDA result is supplied.

- **[SH-01](adjudications/SH-01.md)** (corrected): IDLE uses STATUS.ACTIVE becoming low; READY uses STATUS.READY becoming high. They are distinct event predicates and EVENT_ENABLE fields.
- **[SH-02](adjudications/SH-02.md)** (exercise_convention): For this exercise RXWM is true exactly when rx_depth_words > RX_WATERMARK. Use this strict comparison for STATUS.RXWM and the RXWM event predicate. The author selects the explicit greater-than event definition to adjudicate the conflicting reaches wording inside HJSON; this is not blanket HJSON precedence.
- **[SH-03](adjudications/SH-03.md)** (corrected): During unstalled clock generation T_SCK = 2*(CLKDIV+1)*T_core and T_half_SCK = (CLKDIV+1)*T_core. Interpret waveform time units using this half-period.
- **[SH-04](adjudications/SH-04.md)** (corrected): A running divider timeslice spans CLKDIV+1 core cycles: T_timeslice=(CLKDIV+1)*T_core. FSM updates remain subject to the documented enable/stall conditions.
- **[SH-05](adjudications/SH-05.md)** (corrected): COMMAND.LEN is bits [8:0], range 0..511. A data segment transfers LEN+1 bytes; a dummy segment uses LEN+1 dummy cycles as defined by the field.
- **[SH-06](adjudications/SH-06.md)** (corrected): Quad transfer emits the upper nibble [7:4], followed by [3:0], with the source-defined SD lane ordering.
- **[SH-07](adjudications/SH-07.md)** (corrected): Dual output consumes [7:6], [5:4], [3:2], [1:0] in order for each byte. Each shift consumes exactly two bits.
- **[SH-08](adjudications/SH-08.md)** (corrected): TXSTALL/RXSTALL are diagnostic states and do not directly create an event IRQ. Independently evaluate the declared FIFO and other event-enable predicates.
- **[SD-01](adjudications/SD-01.md)** (exercise_convention): The author adopts the coherent four-byte PAYLOAD_SWAP_MASK/PAYLOAD_SWAP_DATA contract: payload_swap_en enables masked substitution in the first four eligible payload bytes. Unselected bits and later bytes pass through unchanged; shorter payloads only transform bytes actually present. Preserve the documented byte ordering.
- **[SD-02](adjudications/SD-02.md)** (corrected): CMD_INFO.addr_mode refers to ADDR_MODE.addr_4b_en for the configured address-width choice. Bind the actual declared enum values and ADDR_MODE CSR.
- **[SD-03](adjudications/SD-03.md)** (corrected): The declared field is CMD_INFO.read_pipeline_mode[23:22]. Preserve its multi-value enumeration and per-mode timing contract.
- **[SD-04](adjudications/SD-04.md)** (corrected): Upload address presence and width follow the current CMD_INFO.addr_mode enum and ADDR_MODE.addr_4b_en where that enum selects the global width. Upload only the address bytes present in the decoded command.
- **[SD-05](adjudications/SD-05.md)** (corrected): Ingress is 112 32-bit words (448 bytes): payload offset/depth 0/64, command 64/16, address 80/16, TPM-write 96/16, all in words. Egress is 848 words: read buffer 0/512, mailbox 512/256, SFDP 768/64, TPM-read 832/16. Banks have independent address spaces.
- **[CT-01](adjudications/CT-01.md)** (exercise_convention): Use the logical instr_type/cmd_intg/data_intg and rsp_intg/data_intg sidebands with the explicit bench_tl_v1 packed ABI in cadence_contract.md. Historical reserved/parity typedefs do not define this exercise's ABI.
- **[CT-02](adjudications/CT-02.md)** (background_scope): The selected top configuration instantiates uart0..uart3 (four UARTs). UART is whole-chip background and is outside both reduced subsystem DUTs.
- **[CT-03](adjudications/CT-03.md)** (scope_interpretation): The base pinout has 47 muxed pads: IOA=9, IOB=13, IOC=13, IOR=12; direct IOR8/IOR9 are excluded. A 32-bit GPIO vector is not a count of all MIO pads. This constrains AON PINMUX geometry; it is external context in serial-I/O.
- **[CT-04](adjudications/CT-04.md)** (background_scope): The local ROM-key table enumerates seven slots, 0..6. Treat the earlier three-slot count as obsolete background; ROM/key provisioning is outside these exercises.
- **[CT-05](adjudications/CT-05.md)** (scope_interpretation): In serial-I/O use the selected SPI_DEVICE CONTROL modes disabled/flashmode/passthrough with TPM controlled separately. Do not add a legacy Firmware mode without a declared interface. In AON this SPI paragraph is out-of-scope background only.
- **[Q-01](adjudications/Q-01.md)** (exercise_convention): Author convention: CPHA determines the output launch edge (0 trailing, 1 leading); FULLCYC modifies receive sampling latency only, from half a SCK cycle to one full cycle after the corresponding launch. Preserve CPOL edge polarity. This chooses the field's sampling-only description; it is not a proven upstream implementation property.
- **[Q-02](adjudications/Q-02.md)** (exercise_convention): Chip selects are zero-indexed. For this exercise valid CSID satisfies 0 <= CSID < NumCS; CSID=NumCS is invalid and follows the declared CSIDINVAL error handling.
- **[Q-03](adjudications/Q-03.md)** (exercise_convention): Require accepted command conservation, ordered completion and correct READY/backpressure. Freeze candidate capacity/initial state; a universal sixth/seventh-command first-stall cycle is outside this exercise's acceptance model.
- **[Q-04](adjudications/Q-04.md)** (exercise_convention): Use staged SW-to-SPI delivery and atomic committed status at eight-SPI-clock byte boundaries. Hardware set wins over SW clear of the same status bit at one commit; distinct bits update independently. Passthrough gating changes at CSb release. The running-domain delivery bound is in cadence_contract.md.
- **[Q-05](adjudications/Q-05.md)** (scope_interpretation): Apply the control-endpoint post-SETUP special case separately from ordinary OUT flow control: after SETUP clears protocol stall, the guide's set_nak_out/rxenable_out conditions hold subsequent IN/OUT requests in NAK until software prepares the control transfer. Do not extend that special condition to every endpoint/transaction.
- **[Q-06](adjudications/Q-06.md)** (scope_interpretation): Model synchronous accesses at each SRAM port. For this exercise the functional bus/USB clocks share the documented 48 MHz input; preserve their port/domain identities and the separate wake clock. Clock gating and wake handoff still require explicit CDC/reset analysis. The phrase asynchronous dual-port does not require asynchronous read data or unrelated functional frequencies.
- **[D-02](adjudications/D-02.md)** (exercise_convention): cadence_contract.md defines bench_tl_v1 field widths/order, CRC7 polynomial, bit iteration, protected words, known vectors, masks and error policy. This logical bus exercise does not claim binary or SECDED compatibility with upstream TL-UL.
- **[N-02](adjudications/N-02.md)** (not_a_conflict): Partition USB transfer expectations by subtype. Apply the declared OUT_ISO behavior to isochronous endpoints and ordinary ACK/NAK rules to the ordinary transaction types for which they are specified.
- **[N-03](adjudications/N-03.md)** (naming_correction): Program the declared PHY_CONFIG.tx_use_d_se0 field. The theory name use_tx_d_se0 is an alias in prose for the same transmit encoding selection, not a second field.

documents.title: Benchmark author contract: CADENCE
documents.content:
# Cadence standalone execution contract: opentitan-serial-io

Authority: benchmark author, revision opentitan-adjudications-cadence-v2. This is a new digital subsystem
implementation exercise derived from the supplied sources. It is not a binary-compatible
OpenTitan IP port, a production pad-ring implementation, or an upstream regression replay.

Effective rule: Implement the selected subsystem as self-contained synthesizable SystemVerilog with an independent SystemVerilog UVM/SVA environment. Cadence Xcelium/IMC and Jasper/Genus are the execution targets. Upstream RTL, build descriptions and tests are historical comparison material, not required build inputs or an independent golden for this authored contract.

## Implementation and source boundary

The DUT top is `serial_io_subsystem`; all modules listed in integration_profile.json
remain in scope. Implement their documented behavior and register fields under the named
adjudications. Supply ordinary .sv/.svh files, behavioral synthesizable RAMs and explicit
packages. No FuseSoC, DVSim, reggen/topgen, Bazel, Chisel/firtool, Verilator, C/C++ simulator,
software compiler, vendor VIP or upstream source checkout is required to solve this question.
Generated CSR RTL must be checked against the supplied HJSON fields; parsing HJSON is an
authoring aid, not an execution dependency. No encrypted IP or unavailable technology cell
may be introduced. A reused IP is allowed only with its complete pinned portable SV closure.
The saved upstream RTL/UVM/FPV subset has historical provenance, not a qualified Cadence
dependency closure. Its output never silently overrides an authored rule.

Both design and DV consume the same module_graph.json and this contract. Every proposal
identifies owned modules, interfaces, clocks, reset domains and integration obligations.
Do not replace the subsystem with a one-register smoke or count isolated module tests as
integrated closure. Unspecified internal pipelines are design choices, not hidden golden
latencies. Freeze chosen internal interface and assertion contracts before implementation.

## Top-level digital boundary

Use the following signal names; an unsized name denotes one logic bit, `_i` inputs and `_o`
outputs. Every `_no` is an active-low reset output. All vectors descend from N-1 to zero.
The common bus ports are `tl_a_valid_i`, `tl_a_ready_o`, `tl_a_i` (bench_tl_req_t),
`tl_d_valid_o`, `tl_d_ready_i`, `tl_d_o` (bench_tl_rsp_t), declared in bench_tl_pkg.

Additional ports: clk_core_i, clk_usb_i, clk_aon_i, rst_ni; spi_dev_sck_i, spi_dev_csb_i, spi_dev_sd_i[3:0], spi_dev_sd_o[3:0], spi_dev_sd_oe_o[3:0]; spi_host_sck_o, spi_host_csb_o[1:0], spi_host_sd_i[3:0], spi_host_sd_o[3:0], spi_host_sd_oe_o[3:0]; usb_dp_i, usb_dn_i, usb_vbus_i, usb_dp_o, usb_dn_o, usb_d_o, usb_se0_o, usb_tx_oe_o, usb_dppullup_o, usb_dnpullup_o; usb_wake_req_o, usb_wake_ack_i, usb_functional_clock_enabled_i; irq_spi_host_o[31:0], irq_spi_device_o[31:0], irq_usbdev_o[31:0], alert_o[2:0].

IRQ vector bit indices follow the pinned interrupt_list order; unused bits are zero.
Serial alert_o bits are spi_host0, spi_device, usbdev in order and are observed digital
error outputs. They stay asserted until reset after a fatal integrity event and do not
require an unavailable alert receiver package. AON peripheral slots are numbered by
the selected pinmux configuration (75 outputs into the mux, 57 inputs out of it).
All 16 DIO entries retain the generated HJSON geometry; DIO0/1 model IOR8/IOR9,
and DIO2..15 are digital dedicated peripheral pins numbered in order, not extra MIO.
For DIO0/1 use the internal SYSRST ec_rst_l/flash_wp_l outputs; DIO2..15 use
dio_peripheral_data_i/oe_i. All DIO sample outputs apply the configured attributes.
Do not infer analog current, slew delay, metastability immunity or power signoff
from these digital ports. Where a listed generic signal is unused in this subsystem, bind
it by an explicit source-traced design choice, retain it in the shared contract and test
the binding. AON reset leaf vectors use profile.modules order. Each selected
peripheral leaf has LC as its sole reset parent, while rst_sys_no resets the external
CPU boundary; POR asynchronously asserts both. LC assertion propagates to SYS, but
an isolated SYS reset does not assert LC. Release is synchronized in each leaf domain.
Boot vector order is OTP, lifecycle, flash, ROM. Requests remain until acknowledgement;
errors enter the source-defined startup-failure path. Acknowledgements are controllable,
never permanent assumptions. ast_power_good_i and clock_ack_i model digital environment
responses. EDN ack returns one 32-bit word for an outstanding request; lack of ack is
backpressure and edn_error_i rejects that word. Lifecycle production mode disables
debug/DFT access. External wake/reset bits OR with selected source-listed internal
producers; reserved bits are ignored. All these conventions are digital exercise
interfaces, not a claim of the production SoC's exact packed interfaces.

For AON clock_leaf_o and clock_enable_o, bits 0..3 are IO_DIV4_PERI,
IO_DIV2_PERI, IO_PERI, USB_PERI, matching CLK_ENABLES field order. Their roots
are clk_io_i/4, clk_io_i/2, clk_io_i and clk_usb_i respectively. Bits 4..7 are
MAIN_AES, MAIN_HMAC, MAIN_KMAC, MAIN_OTBN from clk_main_i, in CLK_HINTS order.
clock_idle_i bits 0..3 are input idle indications for those four transactional
leaves; honor the source-defined idle qualification before disabling them.
clock_enable_o reports the effective enable and clock_leaf_o the actual gated
clock. clock_ack_i bits correspond to those same eight outputs and are input
acknowledgements from external consumers, allowing withheld/late responses in
the power sequence; never use an ack as the clock waveform or as CSR gate state.
The six selected managers retain an ungated clk_core_i control-plane clock and
their source-defined AON auxiliary clock; the eight gateable leaf consumers are
environment boundaries, not new AES/HMAC/KMAC/OTBN implementation tasks.
extclk_req_o and extclk_hi_speed_o expose the EXTCLK_CTRL request to the AST
boundary; extclk_ack_i is its independently delayed response. The AST BFM drives
the root input frequencies for normal/external-speed modes before acknowledging;
the DUT does not require an analog oscillator or technology clock mux.
jitter_req_o exposes JITTER_ENABLE digitally; characterize request/lock behavior,
not analog jitter spectra. Exercise source clock measurement/timeout on each
provided root and divided IO root with separately driven stop/frequency errors.

## Shared logical bus and integrity oracle (D-02 / CT-01)

The exercise bus preserves applicable TL-UL Get/Put handshakes, masks, ordering and
errors but uses an author-defined `bench_tl_v1` packed ABI. It is deliberately not the
upstream TL-UL binary ABI or SECDED code. The following declarations are normative,
ordered from most-significant field to least-significant field:

```systemverilog
typedef struct packed {
  logic [2:0] opcode, param;
  logic [1:0] size;
  logic [3:0] source;
  logic [31:0] address;
  logic [3:0] mask;
  logic [31:0] data;
  logic [3:0] instr_type;
  logic [6:0] cmd_intg, data_intg;
} bench_tl_req_t;
typedef struct packed {
  logic [2:0] opcode;
  logic [1:0] param, size;
  logic [3:0] source;
  logic sink;
  logic [31:0] data;
  logic error;
  logic [6:0] rsp_intg, data_intg;
} bench_tl_rsp_t;
```

Get=4, PutFullData=0, PutPartialData=1; request param=0. AccessAck=0,
AccessAckData=1; response param=0, sink=0, size/source echo the accepted request.
Sizes 0/1/2 mean 1/2/4 bytes, natural alignment; larger sizes and unknown opcodes
return error without register side effects. Get/PutFull masks select all addressed
byte lanes; PutPartial selects a nonempty subset. A read of a write-only field is
zero; a write to read-only/reserved fields has no effect except source-specified errors.
instr_type=4'b0101 is data and 4'b1010 is instruction; peripheral instruction access
and other encodings return error. On error read data is zero and response integrity
still encodes that response. No write or FIFO pop/push may occur for a rejected request.

CRC7 uses polynomial x^7+x^3+1, initial register 7'b0, no final XOR, MSB-first.
For each input bit b: feedback=crc[6] XOR b; shift crc left by one, discard bit 6,
append zero; if feedback is one XOR the seven-bit value 7'h09. cmd_intg covers
{opcode,param,size,source,address,mask,instr_type} (52 bits), data_intg covers data
(32 bits), rsp_intg covers {opcode,param,size,source,sink,error} (13 bits).
Zero input has CRC 0 and the 32-bit value 1 has CRC 7'h09. Test every single-bit
corruption in each protected word and independently calculated multi-bit examples;
do not claim SECDED properties or require detection of CRC collisions. This supplies
the previously missing interface/algorithm; no held-out RTL mining is needed.

At most four requests may be outstanding; source IDs must be distinct while outstanding.
Transfer occurs only on valid && ready. Producers hold payload stable while stalled.
Responses retire in acceptance order; response backpressure cannot drop/duplicate effects.
The wrapper must return a response within 4096 clk_core_i edges when the target domain is
running and response ready remains high. Clock-disabled targets return an error within
4096 running core edges, rather than waiting for a disabled clock. The bound allows
CSR synchronization with the slow AON domain; source-defined polling/status protocols
still apply and a bus acknowledgement must not pretend a slow operation has completed.
Reset cancels the current
bus epoch, clears accepted-but-unanswered requests and prohibits later stale responses.
The scoreboard records cancellation explicitly rather than counting it as a completed read.

Assign 64-KiB windows in profile.modules order starting at address zero. Low 16 bits
are the source-defined CSR/memory offsets; addresses outside these windows error. These
are exercise addresses, not the whole-EarlGrey memory map. Register reset/field behavior
comes from the pinned files with the named adjudications, not autogenerated answer RTL.

## Clock, reset, timing and physical abstraction

For serial I/O, clk_core_i and clk_usb_i are phase-aligned 48 MHz inputs, and clk_aon_i
is an unrelated 200 kHz input. SPI_DEVICE sck is asynchronous external stimulus up to
12 MHz. USB is full-speed digital signaling; software/USB RAM ports are synchronous
as Q-06 specifies. For AON, clk_core_i is ungated 24 MHz, nominally phase-aligned
with clk_io_i/4 before root-switch/fault tests; clk_io_i is 96 MHz, clk_main_i is unrelated 100 MHz, clk_usb_i is
unrelated 48 MHz and clk_aon_i is unrelated 200 kHz. The AST environment can
stop/change the three functional roots without stopping the core/AON control
clocks. Root frequency measurements use programmed thresholds for these declared
rates; the negative tests deliberately violate those thresholds or stop a root.
These are chosen simulation constraints, not achieved timing or frequency claims.
rst_ni asserts asynchronously; each domain releases through two destination-clock
stages. A stopped functional clock cannot suppress AON wake or reset assertion.
Use behavioral integrated clock-gating models with stable-low enable capture; make
every intentional clock crossing and reset crossing explicit to Jasper CDC/RDC.
Do not declare all crossings false-path to obtain a clean report.

SPI_HOST event IRQ is the enabled OR of current event predicates sampled on a core
edge, registered on the following core edge; enabling an already true predicate
asserts it on that following edge. Error IRQ follows the source's sticky W1C state.
For Q-03, exact first-stall cycle is not an acceptance criterion across valid chosen
pipelines: freeze its own capacity and initial state, then prove conservation, ordered
completion and ready/valid behavior at capacity-1/capacity/capacity+1. This replaces
the unfounded universal sixth/seventh-command latency bin, not a failed functional bin.
For Q-04, on one SPI-domain commit boundary hardware set wins over software clear of
the same status bit; all distinct bits update independently. SW requests cross through
a lossless acknowledged queue; committed status is atomically visible at byte boundaries.
Do not impose a fixed phase-independent SW-to-SPI latency. With both clocks running and
no destination backpressure, queue delivery takes at most eight destination edges.

## AON digital pad and strap convention (D-01 / Q-13)

This section applies only to the AON DUT. MIO order is IOA0..8, IOB0..12, IOC0..12,
IOR0..7, IOR10..13 (47 pads). IOR8/IOR9 are DIO0/1 in that order.
IOC8 is TAP0, IOC5 TAP1, IOR5 DFT0 and IOR7 DFT1.
Any optional generic third DFT strap is tied low in this exercise and sampled/tested
as that constant, not treated as a missing externally driven pin.

The digital pad supports inversion, virtual open-drain, pull enable/select, keeper,
Schmitt selection and input-disable. Native open-drain bit 6 is unsupported and reads
zero; virtual open-drain bit 1 is used. Slew values 0 and 1 are supported (writes 2/3
read 1); drive-strength values 0..3 are supported (writes 4..15 read 3). These rules
apply uniformly to the 47 MIO and 16 DIO pads. CSR fields map by name to attr_i as
N-01 says. All supported attribute reset values are zero except IOC8 pull_en resets
one; unsupported/reserved bits read zero. Input disable returns zero to peripherals,
but raw pad sampling used for wake/straps remains observable. Slew/drive values are
digital settings only: no analog delay/current behavior is part of this problem.
This is an explicit author-chosen digital pad capability table, not an inference
about OpenTitan production IO cells or an excuse to skip real mux/wake/retention bins.

## Independent UVM and Cadence deliverables

Derive TP from the source and these author contracts. Supply a bus agent, peripheral
BFMs, passive monitors, independent register/protocol scoreboards, covergroups and SVA;
use virtual sequences for concurrency, errors, reset interruption, clock stop/restart
and cross-module paths. Drivers may not increment pass/coverage counters on their own.
Use a pure SV UVM implementation supplied with the selected Xcelium installation;
no custom DPI/PLI, Python test runner or upstream VIP is required. A C/ELF program is
not required: exercise CSR transactions directly in UVM.

Deliver complete ordered RTL and TB filelists, include directories/defines/top/parameters,
SDC plus Jasper clock/reset/CDC intent, bounded fairness assumptions, named properties,
checker activity counters and a frozen coverage-bin model. Every macro, package, RAM
initialization file and include must be inside the candidate closure.
No network fetch or code generation may occur during EDA execution. Retain Xcelium logs and native
coverage databases, IMC reports, Jasper lint/CDC/FPV reports and Genus elaboration/
synthesis reports. Identify every tool version and run's input hashes, seed and timeout.
Read tool-specific warnings and failed/aborted assertions; process exit code alone is
not acceptance. A waveform, event heartbeat or generated file is not correctness.

Use `dv_generate_uvm(profile_path='eda/verification_profile.json')` for Cadence-oriented
generation. `eda/cadence_runner.py inspect`, `plan` and `run` consume the candidate's
reviewed `eda/project.json`; `project.example.json` is only a non-runnable template.
The stage command supplies that common kit. Existing LoopX native Vivado build/check
and PicoRV32 closure paths are not the Cadence evaluation path. External EDA events
remain observations until their actual evidence is independently checked.

Freeze all applicable functional bins and exclusions before closure iterations. Require
at least 90% functional-bin coverage and zero checker/assertion failures, with code,
toggle and assertion coverage reported separately. Cross-check an independently authored
SV oracle against the declared examples and error mutations before relying on it.
Historical upstream comparisons are optional supporting evidence; differences from
author conventions are recorded, not silently treated as candidate bugs. No Cadence
elaboration, simulation, CDC, proof or coverage result is supplied by this question pack.
